transcript.content:
I'm trying to determine whether I would be able to see the Moon right now.

I'm in Alice Springs, Australia at 2026-11-10 18:27 ACST (UTC+0930) (2026-11-10T08:57:00Z in UTC), at latitude -23.698 degrees and longitude 133.8807 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 5.086 degrees and its azimuth is 253.378 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 16.793 degrees and its azimuth is 249.764 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 1.32 percent illuminated, 13.169 degrees from the Sun, and 398861.4 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Probably not with unaided eyesight under those conditions.

The Moon is technically above the horizon, but:

- It is only **1.32% illuminated**, an extremely thin crescent.
- Its angular separation from the Sun is just **13.2°**, placing it very close to the bright solar glare.
- The Sun is still **5.1° above the horizon**, so the sky is strongly illuminated.
- The Moon is only about **17° high**, in a bright twilight/daylight sky.

Although the thin crescent may be geometrically visible, its illuminated portion would be very faint and close to the Sun’s direction. An ordinary observer would be unlikely to acquire it visually, even knowing the approximate location. Haze, dust, or small errors in the app’s coordinates or timing would make it still harder.

Also, because the Moon is only 13° from the Sun, **do not use binoculars or a telescope**, and avoid sweeping the sky with optical equipment near the Sun. If you try at all, use unaided vision, look toward the Moon’s stated azimuth—about **250°**, roughly west-southwest—and do not stare near the Sun. A clearer opportunity would be after sunset on subsequent evenings, when the crescent is farther from the Sun and higher or more favorably placed.
